subject: Architecture
title: Stained Glass: Walls of Light
description: A quick, practical guide to Stained Glass: Walls of Light.

hook.text: In medieval Europe, most people couldn't read. Churches taught Bible stories through glass.

buildup.text: Glassmakers added metals to molten glass: cobalt for blue, gold for red, copper for green.

discovery.text: Lead strips called cames held glass pieces together, creating a flexible structural web.

twist.text: The red glass recipe was the hardest to master. Some medieval reds have never been replicated.

climax.text: Sainte-Chapelle in Paris has 6,500 square feet of glass — the walls are almost entirely windows.

punchline.text: They turned sunlight into scripture and stone into stories.

quiz.question: How were stained glass pieces held together?
options: With iron nails driven through each piece
With mortar pressed between the glass

details.summary: Gothic stained glass windows were not just decoration but theology made visible — each panel told biblical stories to a largely illiterate population. The cobalt blues and ruby reds were created by adding metallic oxides to molten glass, producing colors that have remained vivid for over 800 years.
details.whyItMatters: Stained glass transformed architecture from shelter into storytelling medium. Gothic cathedrals used light itself as a building material.
takeaways: Windows told biblical stories to a largely illiterate population
Metallic oxides produced vivid blues and reds lasting 800+ years
Light became a building material for storytelling and atmosphere

faq.question: How was medieval stained glass made?
faq.answer: Glass was blown into cylinders, cut open, and flattened into sheets. Metallic oxides were added during melting: cobalt for blue, gold chloride for red, copper for green. Pieces were cut, painted with details, fired in kilns, and assembled into panels using H-shaped lead came strips.

faq.question: Can modern glassmakers reproduce medieval stained glass?
faq.answer: The techniques are known but rarely practiced at medieval quality. Hand-blown glass has natural variations in thickness and color that give medieval glass its luminous depth. Machine-made glass is too uniform.
